name: Throat singing practice

image.caption: Throat singing is a practice where the singer is able to produce two, three, or even more sounds simultaneously. Practicing it for the first time when you are over forty can turn the connections with spirits into a brand new experience.

lead: Throat singing is a family of traditional vocal styles from Mongolia, Tuva and Tibet. Voice-training circles borrow low styles such as Tuvan kargyraa hoping for a lower, richer, more resonant voice.

Singers shape the mouth and throat so selected harmonics stand out, producing two audible pitches at once, and some styles use the false vocal folds as a second sound source. Acoustic and MRI studies of the technique exist, but no study has tested whether practising it changes ordinary speaking pitch.

paras: People learn it from tutorials or teachers, working on low phonation and mouth shapes in short practice sessions, then try to carry the relaxed low placement into speech.
Sources reviewed report no health data on the practice. Voice clinicians generally discuss strain as a concern with any forced vocal technique.

angle.text: Users borrow Tuvan kargyraa and other overtone singing to train a lower, richer voice. The techniques are well documented traditions, but their effect on everyday speech has not been tested.

lead: Throat singing practice, in looksmaxxing and voice-training discussion, refers to using throat-singing or overtone techniques, such as Tuvan kargyraa or Tibetan chant, to train a lower, fuller or more resonant voice. People take it up because voice is part of how a person comes across, and a deeper, richer tone is something many men aim for alongside face and body work.

Overtone singing is a traditional vocal technique in which a singer shapes the mouth and pharynx so that selected harmonics stand out, producing two audible pitches at once.[1] Wikipedia distinguishes it from throat singing, which mostly works on the voice source, though many traditions combine both.[1] Tibetan Buddhist chant often uses the lowest pitches of the voice, and kargyraa adds a second sound source from the false vocal folds.[1]

The techniques come from Mongolia, Tuva, the Altai and Tibet, and Western musicians took them up from the 1960s.[1] Research on the technique includes acoustic and MRI studies of overtone singing, but no study was found testing whether practising throat singing changes everyday speaking pitch.

Vocal-tract shaping; false vocal fold sound source in some styles

paras: Mongolia's main style is khoomii, with variants classified by where resonance is shaped. Tuvan styles include khoomei, sygyt and kargyraa, and the Altai and Khakassia have related kai styles used for epic poetry.[1] Other forms include Sardinian cantu a tenore, Kurdish dengbej, Bashkir uzlyau and South African umngqokolo.[1]

Tibetan Buddhist chanting includes very low-pitched styles; the Gyuke style uses the lowest pitch of the voice.[1] In kargyraa, and in the contra and bassu voices of cantu a tenore, a second sound source comes from the false vocal folds.[1] Composers such as Karlheinz Stockhausen used overtone singing in Stimmung in 1968, and the practice spread to Western music from the 1920s onward.[1]

Wikipedia's article on voice deepening links the male voice's drop at puberty to growth of the larynx under the influence of sex hormones, mainly testosterone, which lengthens and thickens the vocal folds and enlarges resonating spaces in the head.[2] Throat-singing practice works on voluntary control of the vocal tract and low-register technique rather than on these anatomical factors.

Voice-training communities discuss low-register styles as a way to practise vocal tract control and a deeper tone. No published study was found on whether this alters habitual speaking pitch, and Wikipedia's overtone singing article does not discuss effects on voice health.[1]

No studies found on throat-singing practice and everyday speaking voice. Wikipedia's article cites a 2019 acoustic and MRI study of polyphonic overtone singing, which examined how the technique is produced rather than voice outcomes.[1]

timeline.event: Overtone singing begins to reach Western music.[1]
Stockhausen composes Stimmung using overtone singing.[1]
UNESCO recognises Sardinian cantu a tenore as intangible heritage.[1]
Anna-Maria Hefele's overtone singing goes viral.[1]
